steps.text: Part 2 of 4: The knight in a busy position, on the edge and in the corner. This part covers Edge and corner. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

steps.caption: Start in the middle. On d4 the knight has all eight jumps, because every landing square is on the board.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 has eight legal jumps.

steps.caption: One step in from the edge, on b3, two of the eight jumps would land off the board. Six remain.

line.say: One jump brings it back to the middle, where it has eight again.

claims.statement: The knight on b3 has exactly six jumps.

steps.caption: On the edge, on a4, half of the jumps would leave the board. Four remain.

line.say: Even from the edge, one jump toward the middle gives the knight room again.

claims.statement: The knight on a4 has exactly four jumps.

steps.caption: In the corner, on a1, only two jumps stay on the board. Watch how many jumps it takes to get out.

line.say: The first jump leaves the corner.
Black's king steps aside; nothing here threatens the knight.
The second jump reaches the centre, where it has eight jumps again.

claims.statement: The knight on a1 has exactly two jumps.

steps.text: Four examples from the boards you just saw: the middle gave eight jumps, one step in six, the edge four, the corner two. These are examples, not a law: nearer an edge or corner means fewer jumps, and squares next to a corner have three. Counted over all 64 squares [V]: 2 jumps on 4 squares, 3 on 8, 4 on 20, 6 on 16, 8 on 16.

steps.title: Centre, edge, neighbours
steps.prompt: Predict first. Count the knight's jumps in each of the three positions. Which counts differ, and why?

steps.text: [I] A centre knight is stronger because more jumps mean more threats and more retreats. [H] I would treat the edge as a reason to count your exits, not as a ban. *Quick count:* start at the square two up and one right, then go clockwise round the knight: eight stops, none missed. Cross out each stop that is off the board or holds your own piece.

steps.caption: The knight starts on a light square. After one jump it stands on a dark square, after the next on a light one again. Every jump changes the colour of the square, so a knight on a light square attacks only dark squares.

claims.statement: The knight on b1 has exactly three jumps.
The knight can jump to c3.

steps.caption: This knight on h4 is on the edge. Four jumps are possible, but its own pawns on f3 and g2 take two of them away. Two are left.

line.say: From g6 the knight has plenty of exits again, towards the middle. An edge knight is cramped, not lost.

claims.statement: The knight on h4 can go to exactly f5 and g6.

steps.caption: Black's knight is on a8 with two jumps, b6 and c7. The white pawn on a5 attacks b6 and the rook on c1 attacks c7. The bishop on f3 attacks the knight itself.

line.say: The pawn takes it. Both exits lead into an attack, so the knight is trapped.

claims.statement: The knight on a8 has exactly two jumps.
One white piece attacks the knight.

steps.caption: Take away the white pawn on e5 and the same knight has an exit. f6 is attacked by nothing, so the knight can jump there and be safe.

line.say: f6 is free of attackers, so the knight escapes toward the middle.

claims.statement: The knight on h5 has three jumps.
The pawn on e3 attacks f4.
The pawn on h2 attacks g3.
